analysis.one_liner: Lets health insurers sell individual policies nationwide under the rules of a single state they choose.
analysis.headline: The House Energy and Commerce Committee reported the bill on a 24–23 vote in February 2006, but it never reached the House floor and died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let a health insurer pick one state as its 'primary state' and sell individual health insurance in any other state under that state's laws. Insurers would be exempt from the buyer's own state's coverage requirements, rate rules, and most consumer protections, keeping only a federal floor on solvency, external review, and some renewal protections. The buyer's state could still collect taxes and police fraud and insolvency, but could not enforce its own health insurance mandates or price rules on these policies.
analysis.who_benefits: Health insurers, which could sell one product nationwide under the rules of whichever state they designate, and healthier individual buyers who could get lower premiums in exchange for plans stripped of state-mandated benefits and protections.

how_it_helps.text: Lets an insurer designate one state as its 'primary state' and sell individual policies in any other state under that state's laws, exempt from the second state's insurance rules except for taxes, registration, financial examinations, fraud and unfair-claims rules, and external review.
Includes a federal floor: an insurer cannot sell into another state if that state's regulator does not use a risk-based capital formula, or unless an independent external review process exists.
Bars an insurer from re-rating an individual at renewal based on health status or the individual's past or expected claims.

Requires a bold-print notice telling buyers the policy 'may be less expensive' because it is not subject to all of their own state's coverage mandates, consumer protection laws, or rate-change restrictions.

analysis.who_pays: People who need comprehensive coverage — especially those with pre-existing conditions — would face the bill's own acknowledged risk that healthier buyers leave state pools, and buyers of these policies would lose their own state's protections, with enforcement shifted to the insurer's chosen home state.
analysis.who_pays_short: People needing comprehensive coverage; state regulators

drawbacks.text: Buyers in a secondary state would give up their own state's coverage mandates, consumer protection laws, and rate-change limits — the bill's required notice tells buyers the policy 'is not subject to all of the consumer protection laws or restrictions on rate changes of the' home state.

The bill orders a Government Accountability Office study of the effects on premiums and coverage for people with pre-existing conditions — an acknowledgment in the bill itself that cheaper plans for healthy buyers could come at the expense of sicker residents left in state risk pools.

The insurer's chosen primary state has sole jurisdiction to enforce the rules governing these policies; the buyer's state can only notify the primary state if coverage fails to comply, weakening local accountability.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The promise was cheaper individual policies for some buyers, mainly healthier ones. The cost was shifting regulatory power from the buyer's state to the insurer's chosen state and hollowing out state benefit mandates and rate protections; the bill's own disclosure requirement shows its drafters expected buyers to give up protections in exchange for lower price. People with medical problems who need comprehensive coverage would likely face higher costs as healthier people exit state pools.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared the House Energy and Commerce Committee by a single vote in 2005, was reported to the House floor in February 2006, sat on the House calendar for nearly a year, and never came up for a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Shadegg introduced the bill on May 12, 2005, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
After a subcommittee hearing, the full committee marked the bill up on July 20, 2005 and ordered it reported as amended by a narrow 24–23 vote.
The committee formally reported the bill with an amendment on February 16, 2006, and it was placed on the Union Calendar, the list of bills ready for House floor action.
No further action was taken; the bill never received a vote in the House or Senate and expired when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State insurance regulators kept their authority over individual health insurance sold to their residents, and policyholders kept the benefit mandates, rate rules, and consumer protections of their own states.

for.name: Rep. John Shadegg
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gathered 72 cosponsors across two years.

for.name: 72 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, with additional members signing on as sponsors in February 2006.

for.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
for.what_they_did: Marked up the bill, ordered it reported as amended 24–23, and reported it to the House floor in February 2006.

against.name: 23 House Energy and Commerce Committee members
against.role: Committee members who voted against reporting the bill
against.what_they_did: Voted no when the committee ordered the bill reported, producing the narrow 24–23 margin.

against.name: State insurance regulators
against.role: Regulators who would lose authority over out-of-state individual policies
against.what_they_did: Opposed interstate sale of health insurance that strips the buyer's state rules, a position widely reported during the repeated congressional debates over selling insurance across state lines.

sides.party_line_note: 71 of the 72 cosponsors were Republicans, and the committee reported the bill on a near party-line 24–23 vote, with the committee's Democrats in opposition; the one Democratic cosponsor on the list had his name added and removed within days in June 2005.

industries.note: The bill would let insurers sell one stripped-down product nationwide under the rules of a state they choose, shedding other states' benefit mandates and rate limits. Healthier buyers would get cheaper plans, but sicker people left in state-regulated pools would likely face higher costs — a trade-off the bill's own required GAO study was designed to measure.

States would lose the power to enforce their own individual-market insurance rules against policies sold to their residents, keeping only taxes, solvency checks, and fraud enforcement; the insurer's chosen primary state would have sole enforcement jurisdiction.

States could no longer require out-of-state policies to be countersigned by a local resident agent, reducing local agents' role, though states could still license and compensate agents without discriminating against nonresidents.
